new.definition_beginner: A hill is a small group of seeds planted together in one spot. Once the seedlings come up, you remove the weaker ones and keep the strongest one to three plants. Snip or pinch off the extras instead of pulling them, so you don't disturb the roots of the plants you keep. Some guides raise the soil into a low mound for each hill so extra water drains away. Others treat a hill as just the group of plants, with no mound. The distance between hills is measured from one planted group to the next.
new.definition_seasoned: Hill: several seeds sown together in one spot, with the spots set at regular intervals. After emergence, each hill is thinned to its strongest plants: one or two in NC State's handbook, two or three in the CSU and Purdue guides, and one to three in NMSU's. Clip or pinch the extras rather than pulling them, to avoid damaging the roots of the seedlings that stay (NC State, CSU). Sources differ on whether a hill is raised. CSU uses hills or mounds to drain excess water away from seedlings. UGA's pumpkin guide raises the soil a few inches into a gentle mound for drainage. Purdue forms a low, broad hill about 8 to 10 inches high. UGA's home gardening bulletin defines a hill as a cluster of plants rather than a mound of soil. NMSU sows each hill in a hole made with a hoe. Hill spacing is the distance from one hill to the next.

new.definition_beginner: Hilling means piling soil up around plants as they grow. Potatoes are hilled so the potatoes growing near the surface stay covered, because light turns them green. Leeks are hilled to grow a longer white stem. Some carrot varieties push the tops of their roots up out of the soil. Hilling soil around them keeps the roots from turning green. Very tall corn can be hilled to help keep it from blowing over. The mound you build around potato plants is also called a hill.
new.definition_seasoned: Hilling: drawing soil or compost up around growing plants, usually several times a season. For potato, UMN starts when stems are about a foot tall and hills once or twice more, building six to eight inches of soil in total. Hilling keeps shallow tubers out of the light so they don't turn green. More buried main stem also means more stolons. NMSU keeps at least three-quarters of the foliage above the soil line. Leeks get 2 to 3 inches of soil two or three times a season for a longer blanched shaft (USU). On carrot varieties that push their root tops out of the soil, hilling keeps the roots from turning green (UMN). On very tall heirloom dent corn, hilling plus wider spacing helps keep plants from blowing over (Clemson). The trench method replaces mounding: plant in a shallow trench or furrow and fill it in as plants grow (UMN, NMSU). The hilled mound on potatoes is itself called a hill. Planting "in hills" is a different practice, even though NC State's handbook calls it hilling too.
